Villany
vil'la-ny
n. (extreme wickedness; baseness of conduct; a vile act)
Old French vilenie, from vilain, a serf or peasant attached to a villa — the word's descent from a social class to a moral judgment is one of the ugliest in English. Scripture, by contrast, uses it strictly of conduct.

Biblical Definition

The Authorized Version spells it with one l and uses it twice, both for wickedness that has stopped hiding. Isaiah places it in a prophecy about the day when names will finally match things: “The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful” (Isa 32:5), and then “For the vile person will speak villany, and his heart will work iniquity, to practise hypocrisy, and to utter error against the LORD, to make empty the soul of the hungry, and he will cause the drink of the thirsty to fail” (Isa 32:6). Read the sequence: speech, then heart, then hypocrisy, then error against God, then the hungry go empty. Isaiah traces villany from the mouth to the stomach of a poor man, and insists the two ends are the same sin. Jeremiah's use is equally concrete: the false prophets “have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours' wives, and have spoken lying words in my name” (Jer 29:23). Again the pattern — adultery and false prophecy named in one breath, because a man who will lie about God will lie about anything. Villany in Scripture is never merely a private vice; it always reaches somebody.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines villany as extreme depravity; atrocious wickedness; and an act of deep depravity.

expand to see more

VIL'LANY, n. [from villain.]

1. Extreme depravity; atrocious wickedness.

2. An act of deep depravity.

To fill the measure of thy villanies.

3. The act of a villain; a crime. The vile person will speak villany. Isa. 32. The word descends from villain, originally a feudal tenant, and became a moral term by the world's contempt.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 32:6 — "For the vile person will speak villany, and his heart will work iniquity, to practise hypocrisy, and to utter error against the LORD, to make empty the soul of the hungry, and he will cause the drink of the thirsty to fail."

Jeremiah 29:23 — "Because they have committed villany in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbours' wives, and have spoken lying words in my name, which I have not commanded them; even I know, and am a witness, saith the LORD."

Isaiah 32:5 — "The vile person shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful."

Proverbs 6:12 — "A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth."

Modern Corruption

The age has abolished the category of the villain, keeping only the categories of the sick and the misunderstood.

expand to see more

Contemporary moral vocabulary has almost no room left for villany. Wickedness is reclassified as pathology, upbringing, or systemic effect, and the man himself becomes a site where causes met. There is a real truth being abused here — sin does have a history, and providence does place men in circumstances. But Isaiah 32:6 locates the engine in the heart: his heart will work iniquity. Remove that and you have removed the possibility of repentance along with the possibility of guilt, and the man who is only a product cannot be forgiven, because there is no one there to forgive.

Isaiah 32:5 names the opposite corruption and it is the one the prophet expects to last longest: the vile person called liberal, the churl said to be bountiful. Wickedness with a good press. The day of the Lord is described in part as the day the labels come off. Until then the church's duty is the unfashionable one of calling things by their names, which is why the Reformed pulpit has always preached the law before the gospel — not to produce despair, but because a man who has never been told he is a villain has never been told the truth he needs in order to be saved.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nebalah (H5039), senseless wickedness, disgraceful folly; nabal (H5036), fool, vile person; Old French vilenie.

expand to see more

Hebrew nebalah (H5039) — disgraceful folly, outrage; the word for Dinah's violation in Genesis 34:7 and for villany in Isaiah 32:6.

Hebrew nabal (H5036) — the fool, the vile person; the same root that names Abigail's husband, and Abigail says the name fits.

Hebrew aven (H205) — iniquity, trouble; his heart will work iniquity, Isaiah 32:6.

Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood; the lying words spoken in the LORD's name, Jeremiah 29:23.

Old French vilenie, from vilain — a villa-tenant; a class term that the world turned into a moral one.

Usage

"“The vile person will speak villany” — and the hungry soul goes empty; one sin, both ends."

"“Shall be no more called liberal” — the day the labels come off."

"“Committed adultery… and have spoken lying words in my name” — named together, and rightly."
